questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the tension between reliability work and feature velocity as 'structural' rather than a matter of attitude?
options: A team has a fixed number of engineering hours per quarter, and reliability work and feature work both draw from that same finite capacity
Reliability engineers are contractually forbidden from writing feature code
Feature teams are legally required to ignore reliability metrics
The tension only exists in companies that use a specific project management tool
questions.explain: It's a fixed-capacity problem: the same pool of engineering hours has to cover both reliability work and feature work, so the two compete no matter how much either team cares about the other's goals.

questions.q: What does the lesson say actually happens if an organization just resolves the reliability-vs-features tension by fiat ("just do both")?
options: The tradeoff disappears because both goals are achieved simultaneously
The capacity problem doesn't go away — the tradeoff still gets made, just implicitly and inconsistently, usually favoring whichever pressure is loudest that week
Engineers automatically work unpaid overtime to cover the gap
The SLO is automatically recalculated to require less reliability work
questions.explain: Ignoring the structural tension doesn't resolve it; it just means the tradeoff happens anyway, inconsistently and implicitly, instead of being made deliberately.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the actual contribution of the error budget concept — what makes it a mechanism and not a slogan?
options: It eliminates the need for an SLO entirely
It guarantees a service will never have an outage
It automatically fires engineers who exceed the budget
It turns the reliability-vs-velocity tradeoff into a concrete, pre-agreed number both sides can act on, instead of an argument about whether a team is being reckless or conservative
questions.explain: The error budget is a spendable, quantified amount of allowed unreliability. Both sides agree to it in advance, so the decision to slow down or speed up is answered by data rather than by argument.

questions.q: In a team that actually uses error budgets as a working practice (not just a dashboard), what happens when the budget is burning too fast?
options: Risky feature launches get paused and priority shifts toward the reliability work causing the burn, as a pre-agreed trigger rather than an ad hoc punishment
The team quietly ignores it until the next incident forces a conversation
The SLO target is lowered retroactively so the budget looks healthy again
Nothing changes, since the budget is only for executive reporting
questions.explain: A real error-budget practice treats a fast burn as a pre-agreed trigger: launches pause, and reliability work gets reprioritized, because everyone agreed in advance what 'spent too fast' means and what follows.

questions.q: What does the lesson say a healthy error budget surplus should actually license, and why does this half of the mechanism get ignored?
options: It should be banked silently and never mentioned, since a surplus means nothing changed

It licenses taking on more real risk — a riskier launch, deprioritizing reliability work the data says isn't needed yet — and it gets ignored because teams treat a surplus as a passive good outcome instead of an active decision
It should trigger an immediate reduction in the SLO target
It means the error budget was set incorrectly and needs recalculating
questions.explain: The error budget mechanism works both directions: surplus budget is real, data-backed permission to take more risk and move faster, not just something to quietly note and move past.
